Victoria. Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 to 1901, and Empress of India from 1876. Her sixty-three-year reign, known as the Victorian Era, was a period of immense industrial, political, scientific, and military change, as well as the height of the British Empire's global power and prestige.

Victoria adopted the title Empress of India in 1876, a move championed by her favorite prime minister, Benjamin Disraeli, who understood her desire for imperial grandeur. Yet her most defining personal experience came with profound tragedy. She wore black mourning attire for the final forty years of her life following the premature death of her beloved husband, Prince Albert, in 1861. This long mourning shaped not only her appearance but the culture of the entire nation.

She was known as the Grandmother of Europe because her nine children married into royal families across the continent, spreading both wealth and, unfortunately, the genetic trait of hemophilia through European nobility. Despite her elevated position, Victoria remained vulnerable to violence. She survived at least seven assassination attempts during her reign, including several shootings. Her sixty-three years and seven months as queen was the longest in British history until she was surpassed by her great-great-granddaughter Elizabeth II, centuries later. Her grandfather had been George III, reigning during her early childhood, while her relationship with the prime minister William Gladstone was notoriously cold and difficult.
